title: Leopold Aschenbrenner’s AI fund lost most of its value. Now it’s back with $400M.
excerpt: Leopold Aschenbrenner’s AI hedge fund lost most of its value in a July collapse and dumped its portfolio to Citadel. Now it is back with a $400m bet.
content_html:
One of the most talked-about funds in AI is wagering again, barely a week after it nearly blew up. Situational Awareness, the firm founded by Leopold Aschenbrenner, has returned to investing with a $400M bet.

The return is remarkable given what just happened. In July the fund suffered a catastrophic reversal, losing roughly two-thirds of its value in a single month and being forced to dump its holdings.

Aschenbrenner is not a typical fund manager. A former OpenAI researcher, he left in 2024 and published a 165-page essay, also called “Situational Awareness,” arguing that artificial general intelligence could arrive far sooner than most expected.

He turned that thesis into a portfolio. Backed by roughly $225m from names including the Collison brothers, Nat Friedman and Daniel Gross, the fund bet on the “picks and shovels” of the AI boom rather than the model makers themselves.

The strategy worked spectacularly, for a while. The fund piled into data-centre operators, memory chipmakers and power suppliers, and its assets swelled past $20bn as those bets soared, with one measure putting its return at 439%.

The holdings were a map of the boom. They included the cloud provider CoreWeave, Nebius, SK Hynix, SanDisk, Bloom Energy and crypto miners repurposed for AI, the infrastructure everyone assumed would keep climbing.

Leverage turned confidence into fragility. The fund was reportedly running at roughly four-to-one leverage, which magnifies gains on the way up and losses just as violently on the way down.

Then the correction came. When AI infrastructure stocks fell sharply, the leverage triggered margin calls, and the fund was forced to liquidate nearly its entire public equity portfolio, reportedly selling to Citadel Advisors.

The speed was the shocking part. A fund that embodied the AI trade lost most of its value in weeks, a real-world demonstration of how quickly a concentrated, leveraged position can unravel.

The lesson was not about the thesis. Aschenbrenner may well be right that AI needs vast infrastructure; what undid the fund was risk management, the decision to express a correct idea with heavy leverage and little diversification.

The human story adds to the drama. On paper the collapse erased a fortune built in barely two years, a reminder that in leveraged markets, gains that look permanent can prove astonishingly temporary.

It was not an isolated wobble. AI-linked stocks have been jittery for months, with episodes like the rout that followed China’s Kimi K3 showing how fast sentiment can turn on the sector.

The infrastructure names the fund loved are especially exposed. CoreWeave, one of its holdings, has leaned heavily on debt, and its borrowing costs swing with the market’s mood about the durability of AI demand.

The blow-up feeds a louder debate. Skeptics point to comparisons with the dot-com bubble, arguing that valuations and concentration have run ahead of what the underlying businesses can yet support.

Regulators are watching the financial plumbing too. The Bank for International Settlements has warned that an AI bust could hit credit markets as hard as 2008, precisely because so much of the boom runs on borrowed money.

Against that backdrop, the $400m bet is a statement. It signals that Aschenbrenner still believes his core thesis, even after the market delivered a brutal lesson about how to express it.

There is a logic to buying after a crash. If the underlying demand for AI infrastructure is real, then a forced, leverage-driven sell-off can leave good assets cheap, and a fund with dry powder can pounce.

The risk is that the lesson has not been learned. Betting big again so soon, in the same volatile corner of the market, invites the question of whether anything has changed beyond the size of the position.

Whether it is conviction or defiance is the open question. Returning so soon suggests the fund sees the sell-off as an opportunity rather than a verdict, a wager that the AI build-out’s stumble is temporary.

content_html_zh:
人工智能领域最受关注的基金之一在差点破产后不到一周，又开始下注了。 Leopold Aschenbrenner 创立的 Situational Awareness 公司已重新投入 4 亿美元的投资。

考虑到刚刚发生的事情，回报是显着的。 7月份，该基金遭遇了灾难性逆转，一个月内损失了约三分之二的价值，并被迫抛售所持股份。

阿申布伦纳并不是一位典型的基金经理。 他曾是 OpenAI 研究员，于 2024 年离职，并发表了一篇 165 页的论文，也称为“态势感知”，认为通用人工智能的到来可能比大多数人预期的要早得多。

他将该论文变成了一个作品集。 该基金得到了科里森兄弟、纳特·弗里德曼 (Nat Friedman) 和丹尼尔·格罗斯 (Daniel Gross) 等约 2.25 亿美元的支持，押注于人工智能繁荣的“镐和铲子”，而不是模型制造商本身。

这一策略在一段时间内取得了惊人的效果。 该基金大举投资数据中心运营商、内存芯片制造商和电力供应商，随着这些押注的飙升，其资产已突破 200 亿美元，其中一项指标显示其回报率为 439%。

这些资产是繁荣的地图。 其中包括云提供商 CoreWeave、Nebius、SK Hynix、SanDisk、Bloom Energy 以及针对人工智能重新调整用途的加密矿工，每个人都认为基础设施将继续攀升。

杠杆将信心变成了脆弱性。 据报道，该基金的杠杆率约为四比一，这会放大上涨时的收益和下跌时的损失。

然后纠正来了。 当人工智能基础设施股票大幅下跌时，杠杆引发了追加保证金通知，该基金被迫清算几乎整个公共股票投资组合，据报道将其出售给了 Citadel Advisors。

速度是令人震惊的部分。 体现人工智能交易的基金在几周内损失了大部分价值，这在现实世界中证明了集中的杠杆头寸可以多么迅速地瓦解。

这节课不是关于论文的。 阿申布伦纳（Aschenbrenner）认为人工智能需要庞大的基础设施，这很可能是正确的。毁掉该基金的是风险管理，即用高杠杆率和很少的多元化来表达正确想法的决定。

人类的故事增添了戏剧性。 从表面上看，这场崩盘抹掉了不到两年积累的财富，这提醒人们，在杠杆市场中，看似永久的收益实际上可能只是短暂的。

这并不是一次孤立的波动。 几个月来，与人工智能相关的股票一直紧张不安，中国 Kimi K3 之后的暴跌等事件表明，该行业的情绪转变有多快。

该基金喜爱的基础设施名称尤其受到关注。 其持有的公司之一 CoreWeave 严重依赖债务，其借贷成本随着市场对人工智能需求持久性的情绪而波动。

这次爆炸引发了更激烈的争论。 怀疑论者将其与互联网泡沫进行比较，认为估值和集中度已经超出了基础业务的支撑能力。

监管机构也在关注金融管道。 国际清算银行警告称，人工智能泡沫破灭对信贷市场的打击可能会像 2008 年一样严重，因为繁荣的大部分资金都是借来的。

在此背景下，4 亿美元的赌注是一个声明。 这表明阿申布伦纳仍然相信他的核心论点，即使在市场就如何表达这一论点提供了残酷的教训之后。

崩盘后买入是有逻辑的。 如果对人工智能基础设施的潜在需求是真实的，那么杠杆驱动的强制抛售可以让优质资产变得便宜，而拥有干粉的基金可以猛扑。

风险在于我们还没有吸取教训。 这么快就在市场同样动荡的角落再次大举押注，引发了一个问题：除了头寸规模之外，是否还有什么变化。

是坚信还是反抗，这是一个悬而未决的问题。 如此迅速地回归表明该基金将抛售视为一个机会而不是一个判决，押注人工智能建设的挫折只是暂时的。
